Title: Brand Protection in Indonesia: Addressing the Threat of Counterfeit Products and Reputational Damage
Author: Putri Pertiwi
Content:
In a warehouse on the outskirts of the city, hundreds of branded bottles were neatly lined up. At first glance, nothing seemed suspicious. However, after a closer inspection by Integrity Indonesia’s investigators, the signs became visible: slightly different seals, labels that looked too flawless, and bottle content that are nothing like the genuine product.

This is not an isolated incident. This is the reality of counterfeit alcoholic beverages in Indonesia today.

In light of the phenomenon, as part of Integrity Indonesia’s 25th anniversary celebration, we interviewed one of our investigation analysts who holds the Certified Fraud Examiner (CFE) credential. After years of handling counterfeiting cases, she has witnessed firsthand how the circulation of counterfeit products has become a serious threat to brand owners, consumers, and market trust.

The Scale of the Problem Cannot Be Ignored

Although there are no official statistics that comprehensively record the total circulation of counterfeit alcoholic beverages in Indonesia, enforcement data from the Police and Customs authorities compiled from various media reports paints a concerning picture:

  • Banyuasin (2026): The South Sumatra Regional Police raided a home-based operation in Banyuasin that had produced more than 20,000 bottles of counterfeit branded alcoholic beverages.
  • South Kalimantan (2025): Authorities seized 1,399 bottles of counterfeit branded adulterated alcohol.
  • Bogor (2021): Police confiscated hundreds of counterfeit imported liquor bottles of various brands, along with materials and equipment used to manufacture fake alcoholic beverages.

“A combination of factors has fueled the widespread proliferation of counterfeit alcohol, including strong market demand. In fact, underage individuals have already been found consuming alcoholic beverages,” our analyst explained.

She also noted that well-known branded and premium imported alcoholic beverages are frequently targeted because they already enjoy strong consumer trust and command high retail prices. These substantial profit margins make alcohol counterfeiting an attractive illicit business.

Modus Operandi: More Sophisticated Than Many Realize

Many people assume that counterfeit alcohol simply involves refilling used bottles with cheap liquids. In reality, the operation is far more organized.

Based on Integrity Indonesia’s investigative experience, counterfeiters often have established networks that supply used authentic bottles. These bottles are collected from bars, restaurants, and nightclubs, then cleaned, refilled with adulterated liquids, and resealed using specialized equipment.

“If counterfeiters are sufficiently sophisticated, they also use equipment that enables them to replicate alcohol seals almost identically to the originals, complete with excise labels that appear authentic,” she explained.

Fieldfindings typically confirm this modus operandi. In addition to counterfeit products, investigators often discover used authentic bottles, bottle-sealing machines, and production materials that frequently fail to meet food-grade standards.

Perhaps the most concerning aspect of this scheme is its distribution aspect having expanded into digital channels. Counterfeit alcoholic beverages are now openly sold on online marketplaces, taking advantage of limited seller verification procedures. Offline, nightclubs have become major distribution points, where both genuine and counterfeit products are sometimes sold simultaneously to maximize profits.

How Anti-Counterfeiting Investigations Work

Effective enforcement and brand protection efforts always begin with a structured process that generally includes the following steps:

1. Market Monitoring

Integrity’s investigation team first examines online channels to identify stores offering imported products at suspiciously low prices. The clearest initial red flag is a selling price that falls significantly below market standards.

2. Test Purchase

Once preliminary indicators are identified, the team conducts a test purchase. Investigators equipped with in-depth product knowledge will identify anomalies such as:

  • Bottle seals and weight
  • Liquid color
  • Aroma that does not match the authentic product profile

When necessary, Integrity also possesses specialized equipment capable of comparing the characteristics of the purchased liquid with those of the authentic product. This analysis helps strengthen indications of counterfeiting before the investigation proceeds to the next stage.

3. Field Investigation and Legal Enforcement

Using shipping information, the team traces the physical location of the producer. This process requires considerable expertise in building trust within high-risk environments.

Once the production site has been confirmed, Integrity collaborates with authorities, including Customs and the Police, to carry out raids. All findings are subsequently documented in a comprehensive investigation report for the brand owner.

The Impact on Brand Owners: More Than Financial Losses

When counterfeit products circulate in the market, the consequences extend far beyond loss in sales. Brand reputation becomes the primary stake.

“When we conduct a raid and it receives media coverage, they often do not mention ‘counterfeit alcoholic beverages.’ Instead, they directly mention the brand name that was counterfeited. Media narratives are beyond our control,” the analyst explained.

This means that every news report about counterfeit alcohol raids indirectly associates the affected brand with the word “fake” in consumers’ minds, even though the brand itself is the victim. In more severe cases, counterfeit products made with non-food-grade materials can cause serious health consequences for consumers, potentially triggering a far deeper reputational crisis.

Counterfeiting threats can emerge from unexpected sources and brand protection cannot be purely reactive.

Three Strategic Brand Protection Recommendations

Based on years of field experience, our analyst outlined three critical measures every brand owner should consider:

  1. Conduct consistent online and offline market monitoring. Market monitoring is not a one-time activity but an ongoing process. Online marketplaces must be monitored regularly, as they have become primary entry points for counterfeit products.
  2. Educate consumers about authorized distribution channels. Consumers who know where to purchase genuine products represent the most effective first line of defense against counterfeiting.
  3. Build a collaborative brand protection ecosystem. Effective protection requires cooperation among brand owners, professional investigation partners, authorities, and digital platforms to limit the operational space available to counterfeiters.

Brand Protection Is Essential for Every Industry

The counterfeit alcohol cases described above illustrate how reputations built over many years can be undermined by counterfeit networks. However, there is one important lesson that business leaders should recognize: this threat is by no means limited to the alcoholic beverage industry.

Sophisticated tactics—from utilizing authentic packaging and manipulating seals to exploiting online marketplace vulnerabilities—have become universal methods replicated by counterfeiters in other industries. Even though your company operates in healthcare, cosmetics, automotive parts, apparel, or technology products, the risk of losing customer trust remains the same.

Ultimately, brand protection is not merely an additional cost for certain industries. It is a fundamental investment for any business seeking to safeguard product quality, maintain consumer loyalty, and ensure long-term sustainability in the marketplace.

25 Years of Protecting Brands: A Commitment That Continues to Evolve

Throughout Integrity Indonesia’s 25-year journey, counterfeit alcohol cases have continually reminded us why this work matters. Every counterfeit bottle circulating in the market not only causes financial losses for brand owners, but also has the potential to endanger consumers and erode trust in brands that have been built over many years.

Integrity Indonesia’s brand protection services encompass market monitoring, anti-counterfeiting investigations, and support for enforcement operations, all designed to serve as both the first and last line of defense for your brand in the marketplace. We also actively foster collaboration with authorities through training programs and discussion forums to strengthen the handling of counterfeit products in Indonesia. Because ultimately, a strong brand is a protected brand.

Title: The difference between a private detective and a private investigator
Author: Putri Pertiwi
Content:
The difference between a private detective and a private investigator often confuses many people. Even though both conduct investigations, their objectives, methods, and standards of evidence are not the same.

Imagine you discover something unusual in a monthly financial report—such as irregularities in vendor reports or organizational assets slowly “disappearing” without a clear trace. As part of management, our first instinct is usually to find out what is actually happening.

But when suspicion begins to point toward potential fraud, the next question often arises: who should be engaged to assist with the investigation–a private detective or a private investigator?

Private detective vs private investigator

In a literal sense, both roles conduct investigations. However, in practice these roles have slightly different specializations:

Private detective:

Generally known by the public for handling personal or domestic matters. Their focus is often limited to proving facts for individual purposes, such as locating family members or handling personal issues.

Private investigator (corporate investigator):

Specifically trained to operate within organizational environments. Their focus is on risk mitigation, such as internal fraud investigations, conflict of interest cases, and background checks on business partners (due diligence).

Aspect Private Detective Private Investigator
Main Objective Personal/family matters Compliance & risk management
Methodology Primarily field work Multidisciplinary, including OSINT, digital forensics, and audit
Evidence Standard Individual client satisfaction Complies with legal standards for HR, audit & court processes

This difference is not merely about terminology or case scope. In personal investigations, evidence is usually sufficient to provide certainty for individuals. However, in an organizational context, evidence must meet stricter standards because it is often used for management decisions, HR processes, audits, and even legal disputes.
This is where a professional investigative approach becomes essential.

Why must evidence “speak” systematically?

In an organization, findings are useless if they cannot serve as a valid basis for decision-making. Corporate frauds are often executed carefully by individuals who understand system loopholes. That is why professional investigators use broader approaches:

  • Data analysis
    They do not only rely on field observations but also analyze transaction patterns or suspicious documents systematically.
  • Digital forensics
    In the digital era, traces of fraud are often left on electronic devices. Professional investigators know how to extract this data without damaging it, ensuring the integrity of evidence is preserved.
  • Investigative interviews
    This is not ordinary questioning, but a structured technique to extract information while respecting individual rights within the workplace.

Legal aspects and risks in Indonesia

This is the most critical part for management. In Indonesia, investigative activities must be conducted carefully to avoid legal backlash.

Compliance with applicable laws

Indonesia does not yet have specific regulations explicitly governing the private detective profession as seen in some other countries. However, investigative activities must still comply with existing laws, including:

  • Personal Data Protection Law (UU PDP)
  • Criminal Code provisions related to privacy
  • Civil and criminal laws related to access to information

Chain of custody

In the professional world, it is not enough for evidence to simply “exist.” Evidence must have a clear trail: who found it, how it was stored, and when it was obtained. Without a strong chain of custody, evidence can easily be challenged in HR processes or in court.

This means that investigative methods must be both legal and accountable. For companies, this legal aspect is crucial because procedural errors can lead to significant legal risks.

Methodological comparison, from monitoring to forensic analysis

The fundamental difference between private detectives and private investigators lies in the methodology used to collect evidence.

A. Scope and complexity

Personal cases typically involve a limited scope—often involving just one or two individuals. However, organizational investigations may involve:

  • Analysis of thousands of transaction documents
  • Verification of relationships between vendors (hidden affiliations)
  • Audits of internal systems that may contain loopholes

B. Use of technology and intelligence

While traditional detectives rely heavily on field observation, professional investigators use a multidisciplinary approach:

OSINT (Open Source Intelligence)

Gathering information from official databases, company registrations, and digital footprints not easily visible to the public.

Digital forensics

Extracting evidence from communication devices or computers legally without compromising data integrity—critical for court proceedings.

Investigative interviews

Using structured interview techniques to identify inconsistencies in alibis, which often become entry points for uncovering larger cases.

C. Compliance with Personal Data Protection Law (UU PDP)

In Indonesia, any information-gathering activity must be conducted with a high level of prudence to minimize legal risks for the engaging party.

  • Methodology and legal boundaries
    Without standardized procedures aligned with corporate regulations, investigative processes risk exceeding privacy boundaries. This has become increasingly critical since the enactment of Law No. 27 of 2022 on Personal Data Protection (UU PDP), where any data collection must have a legitimate legal basis.
  • Alignment with legal frameworks
    Professional investigators prioritize accountable methods, such as the use of open-source intelligence (OSINT), observation in public spaces, and examination of internal documents that have been formally authorized by the organization. This approach ensures that findings maintain high integrity and can be used as a reliable basis for management decision-making without triggering legal disputes.

Why Choosing the Wrong Service Can Be Fatal

Misunderstanding these roles can lead to long-term consequences for organizations:

  • Invalid evidence
     If investigative methods are deemed unlawful, judges or auditors will reject the evidence.
  • Reputational risk
     Unprofessional investigations (e.g., being detected by the subject or involving intimidation) can damage the organization’s public image.
  • Information leaks
     Investigators without strict confidentiality standards (Non-Disclosure Agreements) can expose sensitive company data.

When Should You Engage a Professional Investigator?

Based on field experience, organizations should consider professional investigative support when facing situations such as:

  • Red flags in financial reports
    For example, inventory discrepancies or unusually inflated vendor costs.
  • Business partner due diligence
    Before entering into investments or strategic partnerships.
  • Indications of conflict of interest
    For instance, when an employee has undisclosed relationships with key vendors.
  • Asset tracing needs
    When embezzlement occurs and the diverted funds’ destination needs to be mapped.

Safe and Legal Investigation Solutions

Although the term “private detective” is more widely recognized, for organizational needs, accountability and methodology are everything. Choosing the right investigator is not just about uncovering facts, but ensuring the process is conducted legally for the future of the company.

Title: Strengthening integrity in Indonesia’s capital markets: what brokerage and securities firms should be doing now
Author: Putri Pertiwi
Content:
Indonesia’s capital markets are entering an important phase of structural reform. Over the past months, the regulatory direction from OJK, IDX, and KSEI has become increasingly clear: the market is expected to become more transparent, more credible, and more resilient, with a stronger emphasis on ownership visibility, free-float quality, investor classification, reporting discipline, and enforcement.

This shift is not happening in a vacuum. It comes at a time when concerns around market integrity, the real quality of public float, shareholder affiliations, account transparency, and compliance discipline have become more prominent. 

In February 2026, OJK, IDX, and KSEI jointly announced an accelerated capital-market integrity reform agenda, including proposals to increase the minimum free-float threshold from 7.5 percent to 15 percent, disclose shareholders holding more than one percent in listed issuers, and expand investor classification granularity. As part of that effort, KSEI also launched a reclassification exercise covering over 35,000 SID records, with data collection targeted for March 2026.

These developments point to a clear direction: regulators are no longer satisfied with formal transparency. They are increasingly focused on whether market structures reflect underlying reality.

For brokerage houses and securities firms, this is a significant signal that compliance can no longer be approached only as a matter of documentation and periodic reporting. 

Firms are increasingly expected to understand the true nature of the accounts they handle, the beneficial owners behind clients and structures, the relationships between shareholders and trading parties, as well as the integrity risks that may arise from weak onboarding, incomplete data, poor monitoring, or internal misconduct. OJK’s KYC framework in the capital markets sector already requires providers to broadly identify beneficial owners, including individuals who ultimately benefit from, control, or transact through securities accounts or non-individual customers.

Furthermore, there is evidence showing  that regulators are prepared to act. In March 2025, OJK revoked the broker-dealer and underwriter business licenses of two securities companies for violations relating to securities-company licensing and reporting obligations. OJK also reported broader capital market sanctions in 2025, including fines, written warnings, and license revocations.

In the February 2026 joint reform release, OJK stated that from 2022 through January 2026, it had imposed administrative sanctions totaling over Rp500 billion on 3,418 parties, including over Rp200 billion in fines on 151 parties for stock-trading manipulation, and that of 42 suspected capital-market crime cases under examination, 32 of them were linked to alleged manipulation schemes such as pump-and-dump, wash sales, and prearranged trades.

This matters because brokerage and securities firms occupy a central position in the market ecosystem. They are not only intermediaries executing transactions, but also gatekeepers for onboarding, account integrity, client due diligence, transaction patterns, internal supervision, and reporting quality. These institutions are often the first place where problems emerge or the last place where they could have been detected before they exacerbate.

In other words, brokerage firms are no longer judged solely on whether processes are followed, but on how far they truly understand the existing risks.

What brokerage and securities firms should be doing now

The first priority is to strengthen client and ownership transparency. Firms should revisit whether they truly understand who stands behind their higher-risk individual and corporate clients, whether beneficial ownership data is reliable, whether client classifications are accurate, and whether their documentation sufficiently identifies nominee arrangements, hidden controllers or affiliated parties. This is particularly important as the market moves toward more granular investor categorisation and greater emphasis on the actual quality of shareholder dispersion.

The second priority is data integrity. The reclassification of SID records highlights a wider issue: account, investor, and shareholder data must be accurate, consistent and usable. Weak or outdated static data creates operational risk, impairs surveillance, affects reporting quality, and can undermine the reliability of ownership analysis. Brokerage and securities firms should therefore review the quality of their onboarding files, client master data, shareholder information, as well as supporting records, and remediate existing gaps before they become regulatory or reputational problems.

The third priority is anti-fraud readiness. OJK’s anti-fraud framework is intended to guide financial services institutions through prevention, detection, investigation and reporting. That means firms should not only have a policy on paper, but a practical operating model: clear escalation channels, red-flag identification, whistleblowing intake, management oversight, case documentation, and investigation readiness. A weak anti-fraud framework can leave firms exposed not only to external abuse, but also to employee misconduct, collusion, document manipulation, conflicts of interest, or failures in supervisory control.

The fourth priority is enhanced detection of suspicious affiliations and abnormal activity. One of the core integrity issues in any capital market is the difference between accounts that are formally separate and investors that are genuinely independent. Firms should be capable of identifying potential undisclosed links between clients, shareholders, directors, employees, introducers, and related accounts. They should also be able to assess whether apparently dispersed holdings may in reality be coordinated, controlled or connected. This is relevant not only for market conduct and surveillance, but also for the credibility of free float and shareholder transparency.

The fifth priority is investigation capability. When concerns arise, firms need a defensible response. Treating allegations, suspicious patterns or internal concerns informally is no longer sufficient. Cases involving employee misconduct, suspicious client structures, possible account linkages, irregular trading patterns, document falsification, misuse of authority, or problematic third parties must be handled in a structured, discreet and evidence-based manner. This becomes even more important in an environment where OJK continues to emphasise enforcement, remediation and governance. 

The ability to conduct investigations effectively is no longer a reactive function. It is a core component of maintaining market credibility.

A practical agenda for firms

In practical terms, brokerage and securities firms in Indonesia should consider a review focused on five areas:

1. Client and beneficial ownership transparency

Reassess KYC, beneficial ownership identification, high-risk client review, and related-party visibility.

2. Data and account integrity

Review SID-related records, account-opening documentation, client master data, and classification accuracy.

3. Anti-fraud and escalation readiness

Test whether fraud concerns, whistleblowing allegations, and suspicious conduct can be escalated and investigated effectively.

4. Affiliation and control risk

Examine whether shareholder dispersion, account independence, and free-float claims are supported by accurate facts.

5. Investigation preparedness

Ensure the firm has a credible process to respond to internal misconduct, client-related concerns, and external allegations.

Where Integrity Indonesia can play a role

As a firm specialised in prevention, detection and investigation, Integrity Indonesia can support brokerage and securities companies in strengthening their integrity framework in a practical and independent way. This may include reviewing KYC and beneficial ownership controls, assisting with high-risk client and affiliation assessments, supporting static-data and file remediation exercises, conducting due diligence on third parties and key personnel, as well as helping firms identify red flags linked to concealed relationships, suspicious conduct or internal misconduct. In addition, a robust whistleblowing program is a must. 

If concerns have already been raised, Integrity Indonesia can also assist with discreet fact-finding and investigations involving employees, clients, beneficial owners, introducers, vendors, or other counterparties. The objective is not simply to identify issues after the event, but to help firms build a stronger capacity to prevent misconduct, detect irregularities earlier, and respond in a structured and accountable manner.

In an environment where visibility is becoming a regulatory expectation, independent insight can provide firms with a clearer, more defensible understanding of the risks they carry.

As Indonesia’s capital markets move toward greater transparency, stronger enforcement, and more robust integrity standards, brokerage and securities firms will be expected to do more than maintain formal compliance. They will need to demonstrate their understanding of the people, structures, relationships, and risks behind the accounts they manage. In that environment, independent prevention, detection and investigation support is likely to become a practical necessity rather thana luxury.

Title: Private investigator in Jakarta, Indonesia: fraud investigation solutions & business asset protection
Author: Putri Pertiwi
Content:
A private investigator is an independent investigation professional who helps companies gather evidence, verify facts, and identify business risks such as internal fraud, conflicts of interest, and asset misappropriation. In a corporate context, these services are also known as corporate investigation or business investigation, which aim to provide objective findings to support management decision-making.

Through a systematic investigative approach, companies can understand risk sources more clearly, strengthen their position in both internal and legal processes, and protect organizational assets and reputation.

In general, business losses may originate from internal or external factors. Internally, risks may arise through misuse of access, claim manipulation, or conflicts of interest. Externally, risks can emerge through vendors, partners, or third parties that lack transparency. In the early stages, these leakages often appear small and considered trivial — vendor costs gradually increase, reimbursement claims become more frequent, or inventory discrepancies remain minor but occur repeatedly.

The Indonesia Fraud Survey 2025 by ACFE shows that corruption is the most dominant form of fraud (47.6%), followed by financial statement fraud  (40.2%) and asset misappropriation. This data indicates that fraud risks can appear in various forms and often involve more than one party.

Therefore, private investigators in Jakarta, Indonesia help companies examine facts, secure evidence, and compile findings systematically. This process is often part of fraud investigations or business investigations aimed at objectively identifying risk sources. By testing data and identifying patterns, an investigation team can help management make evidence-based decisions to protect company assets and reputation.

Challenges in internal corporate investigations

Many companies choose internal investigations because they seem faster and more cost-efficient. However, in practice, they are often more challenging. Why? Here are several reasons:

1) Conflicts of interest reduce investigation neutrality

Internal teams operate within the same system as the investigation target. They also often have working relationships with related parties.

  • Working relationships create assessment bias.
  • Bias weakens objectivity.
  • Weak objectivity makes evidence easier to challenge.

This becomes a major gap when legal teams test the strength of the investigation process.

2) Information leaks faster, evidence disappears more easily

Internal investigations are often quickly spread internally, which can trigger perpetrators to erase traces. Common examples of perpetrator actions include:

  • deleting chats and emails,
  • moving documents,
  • transferring assets,
  • preparing alibis, and
  • pressuring witnesses.

If the investigation becomes known to related parties, they gain time to eliminate evidence. As a result, this weakens the proof process and increases dispute risk.

3) Internal teams struggle to conduct flexible field observations

HR, compliance, or internal audit teams are limited by SOP and defined roles. They also often face difficulty moving flexibly outside the office for field observations.

When field verification is not optimal, the teams cannot fully identify patterns. As a result, investigations fail to capture a complete picture of the methods and perpetrators.

4) Weak chain of custody makes evidence easier to challenge

Evidence for HR or legal purposes is not sufficient simply because it exists. Evidence must have a traceable record. Teams must be able to explain the source, the time of collection, and the storage method of evidence.

If companies fail to maintain the chain of custody, other parties can challenge the validity of the evidence. When evidence is questioned, the company’s position weakens in HR processes, employment disputes, or disciplinary enforcement.

5) Internal witnesses are afraid to speak

Witnesses within companies are often reluctant to get involved due to fear of retaliation or being seen as disloyal. As a result, witnesses may remain silent or provide incomplete information. When witnesses are not open, facts become incomplete. When facts are incomplete, investigations will only produce partial conclusions.

If companies want investigations that are safe for HR and legal actions, they need a process that is independent and well-structured. Independence increases credibility. Credibility strengthens the company’s position. Therefore, involving third parties is often the most logical step.

Why businesses need corporate private investigator services

Businesses need corporate private investigators or independent investigators because risks can harm company assets, operations, or reputation. These risks may originate from internal or external factors, including employees, vendors, and business partners.

Although companies can conduct investigations internally, in many cases an independent approach provides greater advantages. Independent investigators help maintain objectivity, reduce conflicts of interest, and ensure that the evidence collection process is conducted professionally and accountably.

In cases involving potential serious violations or legal risks, using independent investigators often provides stronger credibility compared to internal investigations.

The differences between internal investigations and independent investigators can be seen in the following table:

Aspect Internal investigation Independent investigation 
Objectivity Susceptible to bias due to potential conflicts of interest Independent and objective
Confidentiality Higher risk of information leakage within the internal environment Governed by strict confidentiality and Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA) protocols
Strength of Evidence May have limited legal robustness Collected in accordance with chain of custody standards

A private investigator is not limited to monitoring

Many people assume that investigators only monitor targets. In reality, investigators work through an evidence-building process.

When a company has suspicions, the investigation team begins by identifying and verifying facts. The team then compiles evidence that can be used to support business decisions.

Investigations typically begin with suspicion

Fraud cases rarely begin with a confession. They often start with suspicions arising from early indicators or red flags.

Examples of red flags include:

  • financial reports that do not align with field activities,
  • unusually frequent reimbursement claims,
  • recurring inventory discrepancies, and
  • vendors repeatedly winning contracts despite higher pricing.

In practice, employees often notice red flags first. However, they may also hesitate to report concerns due to fear that their identity will be exposed and that they may face retaliation, such as bullying, exclusion, or even termination.

To address employee reluctance and protect their identity as reporters, companies should implement a secure whistleblowing system.

This means companies need two critical elements simultaneously:

  • A secure reporting channel
  • An independent investigation team capable of following up on reports.

When both elements function effectively, companies can stop misconduct earlier before losses escalate.

When does a business need a corporate private investigator?

A corporate private investigator is needed when a company requires concrete evidence to substantiate suspected misconduct. Based on our experience, these are the most commonly occurring cases in companies:

1) Internal fraud (Employees)

Companies may incur losses when perpetrators exploit internal access. Fraud is also often conducted carefully and systematically. In these cases, investigators can help identify fraud patterns and prepare evidence to support HR and legal processes.

2) Vendor and procurement conflicts

Vendors may collude with internal personnel or manipulate pricing. Therefore, investigators can assist companies in mapping procurement patterns and identify conflicts of interest and indications of collusion.

3) Non-transparent business partners

Business partners may present attractive opportunities while concealing underlying risks. Therefore, as part of corporate investigation, due diligence can help companies evaluate potential partners more objectively and assess partnership risks.

In such situations, investigations help companies verify facts and collect relevant evidence. Once evidence is identified, management has a stronger foundation for making appropriate decisions to protect assets and reputation.

Investigation planning

Professional teams always develop an investigation plan. This plan provides direction and defines methodological boundaries. In both corporate investigations and fraud investigations, planning is a critical stage before evidence collection begins.

The plan typically includes:

  • investigation objectives,
  • scope and timeline,
  • types of evidence required, as well as
  • risks and mitigation strategies.

Common scope of private investigator services in Jakarta for businesses

The following services are among those most frequently required by companies:

A) Monitoring

Investigators monitor targets discreetly and document activity patterns.

Business benefits  of monitoring include:

  • substantiating violations,
  • testing alibis, and
  • mapping meeting patterns.

B) Employee background checks & due diligence

Investigators review the history of specific individuals or entities to assess risk.

Areas that may be examined include:

  • employment history,
  • professional reputation, and
  • potential conflicts of interest.

Background checks and due diligence reduce hiring risks and help protect corporate reputation.

C) Asset tracing

The team helps companies identify asset flows when there are indications of concealment or misappropriation.

  • Assets relate to financial interests.
  • Tracing identifies concealment and misappropriation indicators.
  • Findings can be used to support recovery strategies.

D) Fraud & misconduct investigations

Investigators identify patterns, perpetrators, and supporting evidence.

Examples include:

  • reimbursement manipulation,
  • vendor abuse,
  • embezzlement,
  • procurement mark-ups, and
  • conflicts of interest.

E) Basic digital intelligence

The team analyzes digital footprints to support investigative direction. This analysis helps filter relevant information and guide investigative steps. In certain cases, it may develop into forensic or digital forensic investigation to obtain deeper evidence.

Interviews, a key element in business investigations

Business investigations cannot rely solely on surveillance. Investigators must conduct interviews with witnesses and related parties.

You may ask, “Why are interviews necessary?” This is because perpetrators often leave gaps when explaining details. When investigators test those details, they can identify inconsistencies.

In several cases we have handled, investigative interviews served as a strategic initial step to narrow the investigation scope and obtain essential baseline information. Subsequent stages may involve additional investigative methods if required, including digital forensics to obtain valid evidence.

Chain of custody: evidence must be defensible

Companies often require evidence for HR, audit, or legal purposes. Therefore, evidence must not only be identified but must also have a clear record regarding its source, time of collection, and storage method.

Professional investigation teams typically ensure this by:

  • storing evidence systematically,
  • documenting collection time and source,
  • maintaining data integrity throughout the investigation process.

With proper collection procedures, evidence becomes stronger and more difficult to challenge when used in decision-making or legal proceedings.

Root cause analysis: findings should strengthen systems

Comprehensive investigations do not stop at identifying perpetrators. They must also identify root causes of fraudulent actions.

Examples include:

  • weak SOPs,
  • overly permissive approval processes, and
  • inadequate vendor controls.

When root causes are identified, companies can improve systems to prevent recurrence.

Yes, private investigators are legal provided the investigation process does not violate applicable laws.Professional investigators are not allowed to engage in actions such as:

  • extortion,

Title: The Role of Private Investigators in the Vendor Due Diligence Process
Author: Putri Pertiwi
Content:
Fraud isn’t always an “inside job.” You can spend millions on internal controls, only to be robbed by the third parties you invited through the front door. This is supported by the research report “Fraud Risk Management 2025” conducted by IIA Indonesia and ACFE, which shows that vendors and external relations are one of the three biggest fraud perpetrators.

Unfortunately, many companies only realize this after losses occur; when money is gone, projects are compromised, or regulators begin asking uncomfortable questions. Yet a large part of this risk can be reduced if vendor screening goes beyond documents and declarations, and involves professionals who know how to uncover what vendors do not always reveal.

That is where private investigators add real value in the vendor due diligence process.

What is Vendor Due Diligence and Its Purpose

Vendor due diligence is a structured way to understand who a company is dealing with before entering into a partnership. The goal is simple: avoid partnering with vendors who could bring legal, financial, reputational, or ethical risk.

This process usually includes reviewing:

  • legal standing
  • ownership structure
  • track record and history
  • financial stability
  • business reputation
  • regulatory and compliance exposure

In practice, this is not just paperwork. It is about understanding whether a vendor can be trusted to handle contracts, money, and responsibilities without exposing the company to hidden risks.

The Role of Private Investigation in Vendor Due Diligence

Private investigation in a corporate context focuses on gathering information that is accurate, verifiable, and useful for decision-making. Instead of relying solely on vendor-submitted documents, investigators look deeper, identify inconsistencies, and reveal risks that might otherwise stay hidden.

In a vendor due diligence process, private investigators can support by conducting:

  • Identity and ownership verification. Ensuring the real individuals behind the company are what they claim to be.
  • Legal and litigation review. Checking whether the vendor has been involved in disputes, fraud cases, or contract violations.
  • Reputation and background analysis. Assessing how the vendor is perceived by partners, the market, and credible public sources.
  • Financial condition review. Identifying whether the vendor is financially stable enough to fulfill its obligations.

With stronger and independently verified insight, management is not forced to rely on assumptions, personal trust, or optimistic expectations. Decisions are backed by facts.

All investigative processes must also comply with applicable laws, including data protection and business privacy regulations. This ensures that the investigation is not only effective, but also lawful and ethically defensible.

Case study: the “perfect” vendor and the hidden interest

In one investigation, due diligence revealed a significant conflict of interest between a heavy equipment manufacturer and the department head of a company that served as its client.

The investigation began when the manufacturer consistently won an unusually high number of tenders. Although the vendor met all technical requirements, its repeated success in securing high value contracts raised concerns among senior management who suspected favoritism or internal influence in the vendor selection process.

This triggered a deeper investigation, which demonstrated due diligence is not merely a formality, but a vital strategy that is essential in uncovering hidden risks and potential conflicts of interest that threaten business integrity.

The investigation focused on several key aspects, beginning with an in-depth review of procurement practices and tender evaluation procedures. Although the vendor repeatedly won tenders based on merit, the investigation uncovered an undisclosed family relationship between the department head and the owner of the vendor.

This lack of transparency violated the company’s conflict of interest policy, which requires employees to disclose family relationships with vendors to ensure objective vendor selection.

Failure to disclose such conflicts of interest typically results in disciplinary action under the company’s ethics policy, with consequences depending on the severity and impact of the violation.

Benefits of Using Private Investigation 

Integrating private investigation into the vendor due diligence process offers many advantages for companies including the following:

  • Transparency and data accuracy. All information obtained is independently verified rather than solely based on documents provided by the vendor.
  • Earlier risk mitigation. Investigators can identify signs of fraud, conflicts of interest, or hidden relationships before collaboration begins.
  • Time and cost efficiency. A targeted investigation process helps companies avoid future legal and financial problems.
  • Reputation protection. By selecting credible vendors, companies safeguard their image and stakeholder trust.
  • Compliance with regulations. A due diligence process supported by private investigation helps fulfill compliance standards such as the Anti-bribery Management System (ISO 37001).

How to Choose a Credible Private Investigator

Not all private investigation service providers have expertise in the corporate field. Therefore, companies need to be prudent when selecting an investigative partner.
Several key factors to consider include the following:

  • Ensure that the service provider has an official operating license and complies with local regulations.
  • Choose a provider with extensive experience in business investigations and vendor due diligence.
  • Review client testimonials and track records.
  • Ensure that they maintain data confidentiality and operate in accordance with privacy laws.

Engaging professional and experienced investigators ensures results that are objective, accurate, and defensible.

Title: Whistleblowing System and Integrity Transformation
Author: Putri Pertiwi
Content:
In commemoration of International Anti-Corruption Day (HAKORDIA) on 9 December, Semen Indonesia Group (SIG) held an internal seminar titled “Strengthening Commitment to Gratification Control and Anti-Bribery Compliance.” The event, which took place on 19 November, is part of SIG’s ongoing educational efforts as a state-owned enterprise (BUMN) to reinforce integrity and enhance the effectiveness of good corporate governance implementation.

HAKORDIA itself stemmed from the awareness among UN member states that corruption brings harmful impacts to social, economic, and governmental development. This awareness eventually led to the establishment of the United Nations Convention Against Corruption (UNCAC) on 31 October 2003. On 9 December, this commitment was realized through the signing of the Anti-Corruption Agreement in Merida, Mexico, a moment later commemorated as HAKORDIA. As of 2023, 187 UN member states have signed the agreement, including Indonesia.

At this year’s HAKORDIA event at SIG, the President Director of PT Integrity Indonesia, Edouard Helfand, serving as SIG’s independent whistleblowing system partner, was present as a speaker to discuss the role of whistleblowing systems in supporting the prevention of violations within the company.

Integrity as Part of SIG’s Transformation

SIG is currently implementing its transformation strategy, “Turnaround Towards Excellence,” which focuses on innovation, collaboration, operational efficiency, and sustainability. In his opening remarks, the President Director of PT Semen Indonesia (Persero) Tbk, Indrieffouny Indra, emphasized that every transformation effort must be grounded in integrity and strong commitment from all members of the organization.

“Transformation is not enough without integrity and heart. Therefore, it requires a commitment of hard work for the advancement of a company owned by the people of Indonesia,” he stated.

The Independent Board of Commissioners, represented by Saor Siagian, also expressed appreciation for the event, considering it a strong reflection of SIG’s commitment to strengthening a culture of compliance. Held in a hybrid format, the seminar was attended by more than 900 participants from various SIG business units and subsidiaries, demonstrating significant interest from SIG in integrity-related issues.

Risks of Gratification and Bribery

The first session was delivered by Ipi Maryati Kuding, Head of Task Force IV of the Anti-Corruption Directorate for State-Owned Enterprises at the Corruption Eradication Commission (KPK). During her session, Ipi highlighted an important point: integrity remains a national issue, and business entities contribute to these challenges. Ipi also outlined various corruption risks, particularly gratification and bribery, that may occur in corporate operations and the potential impacts on reputation and business sustainability.

She also provided practical guidance for individuals in handling gratification, along with mitigation steps companies must implement, one of which is providing effective and trustworthy reporting channels.

Building Trust Through an Independent Whistleblowing System

The next session was delivered by Edouard Helfand, who emphasized the strategic role of whistleblowing systems as fraud detection tools. He explained that various studies show whistleblowing systems are the most effective tools of fraud detection. However, the success of the systems heavily depends on the level of trust whistleblowers have in the system’s independence and confidentiality mechanisms.

According to Edouard, many companies face challenges because potential whistleblowers are reluctant to report due to fear of retaliation or uncertainties about identity protection. Therefore, third-party managed reporting systems offer a solution by providing greater independence and confidentiality, thereby encouraging whistleblowers to come forward.

He further stressed that companies must ensure reporting channels are accessible, secure, and capable of handling reports systematically. Additionally, continuous education and communication with employees, as potential whistleblowers, are essential.

“Having a whistleblowing system is one thing. But if a company does not educate its employees on how to use the whistleblowing system, provides reporting channels that are difficult to access, and fails to investigate the reports received—in other words, if it implements the whistleblowing system merely to meet compliance requirements—then it will not be effective,” he explained.

Canary Whistleblowing System as a Supporting Solution for SIG

In the context of strengthening integrity, Edouard Helfand introduced the Canary Whistleblowing System, a misconduct reporting management service developed by PT Integrity Indonesia. This whistleblowing system complements Integrity Indonesia’s suite of fraud detection services.

Canary is designed to help companies manage reporting independently and professionally while ensuring data security and whistleblower anonymity. Several key features relevant to companies like SIG include:

  • Multi-channel reporting (website, email, hotline, and other channels)
  • Multi-language support for employees with diverse language backgrounds
  • Strong whistleblower identity protection
  • A case management system for easy monitoring and documentation
  • Investigation support tailored to company needs

Canary enables companies to strengthen the implementation of Good Corporate Governance, support ISO 37001 requirements, adopt whistleblowing standards in accordance with ISO 37002, and serve as an early detection tool to prevent violations that could harm the company.

The participation of Integrity Indonesia as one of the speakers in this seminar demonstrates the importance of professional partners in supporting corporate efforts to prevent corruption and gratification. By utilizing independent systems such as the Canary Whistleblowing System, companies can cultivate a stronger reporting culture and ensure more credible and transparent case management.

Title: Fraud Prevention Methods: A Best-Practice-Based Guide
Author: Putri Pertiwi
Content:
Fraud risks continue to rise in line with the digitalization of business processes. Various studies show that fraud schemes are becoming increasingly complex, exploiting system loopholes and weaknesses in internal processes. These studies also highlight that many organizations struggle to detect fraud due to the rapid evolution of the perpetrators’ tactics. In addition, Occupational Fraud 2024: A Report to the Nations by the ACFE (Association of Certified Fraud Examiners) reveals that organizations lose an average of 5% of their annual revenue to fraud.

This situation underscores the need for more comprehensive fraud prevention methods. An effective strategy should not only emphasize internal controls but also ensure that risks are mapped early and that every indication of fraud can be addressed appropriately.

What is Fraud?

Fraud is an intentional act to obtain undue benefit that causes harm to another party. Manifestations of fraud include embezzlement, corruption, data falsification, asset misuse, conflicts of interest, and more.

How to Prevent Fraud in an Organization

1. Fraud Risk Assessment (FRA): The First Step in Fraud Prevention

All effective fraud prevention strategies begin with a Fraud Risk Assessment (FRA). Without an FRA, organizations are unaware of which areas are most vulnerable and which controls should be prioritized.

FRA is a systematic process to:

  • Identify potential fraud scenarios in each business process.
  • Assess the likelihood and impact of each scenario.
  • Evaluate whether existing controls are effective.
  • Determine areas requiring stronger internal controls.

FRA is crucial because threats can emerge from gaps in processes and system access as well as weak oversight. Without an FRA, organizations may rely on generic controls that do not address actual risks.

FRA provides a data-driven foundation for informed decision-making rather than assumptions. Common risks identified in FRA include invoice manipulation, fictitious procurement, system access misuse, conflicts of interest involving vendors, and petty cash embezzlement.

2. Designing Targeted Fraud Prevention Controls

The same report notes that more than half of the fraud cases occurred primarily due to a lack of internal controls. FRA results serve as a complete map that indicates which areas need reinforcement. From there, organizations can design targeted fraud prevention controls. Controls that typically emerge from FRA include:

a. Segregation of duties

Fraud often occurs when one person holds multiple critical roles. FRA helps identify these weak points and restructure workflows.

b. System access restrictions

Fraud incidents can  occur due to excessive system access. FRA helps determine who should have access to what. For example, server rooms should only be accessible to authorized IT personnel, and the use of external devices should be restricted to prevent data theft. 

c. Vendor verification and due diligence

Vendor-related fraud is a common challenge faced by numerous businesses. Through FRA, businesses can investigate potential vendors or current partners.

d. Anti-fraud SOPs and code of ethics

These documents should define workflows, authority limits, reporting mechanisms, and integrity standards for all employees. They must be clear, easy to understand, consistently communicated, and auditable so every step in the process has a traceable trail.

e. Whistleblowing system

The report also shows that more than 40% of fraud cases were detected through tips. In other words, reporting systems are generally effective in detecting fraud.

3. Conducting Fraud Investigation as a Preventive Measure

Fraud investigation is often seen as a reactive measure carried out only after fraud or losses occur. However, various studies and professional guidelines show that investigations actually play a strategic role in long-term fraud prevention.

A proper investigation not only aims to identify perpetrators or quantify losses but also helps organizations understand the system weaknesses that allowed fraud to occur. These findings become the basis for improving internal controls, strengthening policies, and closing previously unidentified process gaps.

a. Proactive Fraud Investigation

Conducted routinely to detect early signs of fraud through methods such as:

  • In-depth audits of high-risk transactions
  • Surprise audits
  • Analysis of employee behavioral patterns

b. Root Cause Analysis

Each fraud incident should be analyzed to determine its root cause. Was it due to weak controls? A flawed organizational culture?

c. System Strengthening After Investigation

Investigation results should guide improvements to policies, SOPs, and technology systems.

d. Importance of Professional Investigators

Investigations must not be performed carelessly, as they involve:

  • Legal considerations
  • Accuracy of evidence
  • Objectivity
  • Potential reputational risks

Working with professional fraud investigators significantly enhances prevention effectiveness.

4. Education as a Core Pillar of Prevention

Many fraud incidents occur not only due to malicious intent but also due to lack of awareness and ignorance of red flags or proper procedures. Why is education important?

  • Enhances the ability to recognize fraud indicators.
  • Ensures compliance with SOPs and codes of ethics.
  • Strengthens the culture of integrity.
  • Reduces procedural errors that perpetrators can exploit.
  • Encourages people to report suspicious activities.

Fraud prevention education must be provided to all parties involved in organizational operations, including employees at all levels and company leadership.

By implementing comprehensive fraud prevention methods as described in this guide, organizations can strengthen resilience, protect their reputation, and minimize financial losses.

Title: Background screening: the importance of official data sources
Author: Putri Pertiwi
Content:
Several pre-employment background screening providers often sell “speed” as their main value, even claiming they can deliver verification results within hours. But, have you ever wondered how they can deliver results that quickly?

In 2022, the case of Taylor v. Inflection Risk Solutions, LLC in the United States sent shockwaves through the background screening industry. Tony Taylor, a Minnesota resident, was denied an Airbnb rental because his background check report stated that he had a felony record.

In reality, the charge had been reduced to a misdemeanor after he completed his probation period. This data error severely affected Taylor’s reputation and opportunities. The case eventually turned into a class action lawsuit, and Inflection Risk Solutions agreed to a settlement of USD 4 million for Taylor and thousands of others who fell victim similar mistakes.

This case is not merely about negligence, it highlights one often overlooked crucial point: the accuracy of data sources is far more important than the speed of results.

The challenges behind pre-employment background checks

Behind every seemingly simple background screening report lies a complex process. Not all data can be accessed publicly, instantly, or through a centralized source.

For example:

  • Education verification in certain countries can only be performed by submitting direct requests to the issuing universities and often requires written consent from the candidate.
  • Criminal record checks in some jurisdictions require specific legal documents and limited access to official databases.
  • Employment history verification sometimes involves direct confirmation from previous employers’ HR departments, which can take several days to obtain.
  • Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs) screening is challenging because political positions can change rapidly, thus requiring continuous data updates.

This is why professional background screening services should not solely focus on speed. Each verification involves legal, administrative, and cross-border communication processes. The results may not be instant, but they should be ethically and legally accountable.

Also read:

Pre-employment Screening: The Medical Check Up of Your Candidate

Reference Check

Between speed and compliance

Some service providers promise screening results within 24 hours. However, such promises often come at the cost of data quality and validity.

A clear example can be found in criminal record checks in Thailand. These checks can only be performed through the Royal Thai Police (RTP) and cannot be fully automated.

When a company uses a background screening service provider, foreign candidates must appear in person at the RTP with the provider’s representative to submit their fingerprints and required documents.

Meanwhile, for Thai nationals, the request can be represented by a third-party provider who submits the required documents directly to the RTP.

Before any check can be performed, a consent letter is a mandatory document that the third party must obtain from the candidate, regardless of nationality. The entire process typically takes 8–15 business days.

If any party attempts to speed up the process using unofficial data sources, the resulting report risks being legally invalid and may violate Thailand’s Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA), which stipulates that personal data can only be collected and processed with lawful consent.

This illustrates why background screening should not be measured solely by how fast the results are delivered, but also by the legality of the data sources and compliance with local regulations.

Compliance with data protection regulations

Beyond speed and accuracy, compliance with personal data protection laws is a crucial component of pre-employment background screening. For instance, the GDPR in Europe and Indonesia’s PDP Law stipulate that personal data may only be processed for legitimate purposes and with explicit consent from the data owner.

This means that every stage of the screening process, from data collection and verification to final reporting, must be conducted transparently and in accordance with lawful processing principles. Violating these principles can lead to legal sanctions and the loss of public trust in both the company using the service and the service provider itself.

Why it’s important to partner with a credible provider

Choosing a credible pre-employment background screening provider means choosing security, accuracy, and compliance. A professional provider will:

  • Use official and verifiable data sources.
  • Maintain transparency at every stage of the process.
  • Comply with both local and international data protection regulations.
  • Deliver accurate, accountable, and actionable reports.

Ultimately, background screening is not about who can deliver the fastest results, it’s about who can be trusted to uphold the integrity of the data and the process.

Title: The future of employment background screening: AI vs human
Author: Putri Pertiwi
Content:
Before the digital era, compliance activities were often associated with long and tedious processes such as piles of paperwork, manual audits that could take months, and slow investigations. For instance, employment background screening once took weeks to complete before the final hiring confirmation.

 Today, artificial intelligence (AI), through applicant tracking systems (ATS), can scan and rank thousands of CVs based on keywords, skill relevance, and company-defined criteria. Thanks to this technology, routine tasks such as CV screening can now be completed in seconds. AI is not merely a tool; it serves as the eyes and brain capable of processing massive volumes of data within a short time.

In many cases, technology has enabled compliance professionals to achieve unprecedented efficiency. Big data analysis is faster, identity verification is simpler, and potential risks can be detected earlier.

Several studies show that more companies are integrating AI into their recruitment systems. One study found that AI excels in analyzing large data sets, improving recruitment speed by up to 70% and reducing hiring costs by 30%.

However, as AI adoption grows, a critical question arises: will this “automation” technology completely replace the human role in compliance, specifically in employment background screening?

Behind the algorithm

AI operates based on data provided by humans. It can analyze, predict, and classify rapidly. Yet despite its evolving capabilities, AI still struggles to understand complex human contexts or provide justifications that consider real-life values and circumstances.

 For example, an AI-based employment background check system might flag a candidate as “high risk” simply due to a three-year employment gap. However, the system does not recognize that the gap could have resulted from personal reasons such as caring for a sick parent or pursuing self-development outside formal education.

Moreover, AI screening systems can misinterpret data. Reuters once reported that Amazon’s recruitment algorithm was biased against female applicants. This was caused by most resumes received over the previous decade coming from male applicants, which led to the algorithm favoring male applicants and treating the word “women” as a negative indicator.

Misinterpretations can also occur in simpler contexts. For instance, an AI system might flag a candidate as a “job hopper” for changing jobs three or four times within two years. However, upon human review, it may turn out that the candidate had worked at startups that shut down due to restructuring or the pandemic. In this case, while AI perceives the candidate as a risk, a human analyst might instead recognize valuable traits such as adaptability and resilience, qualities that are crucial in today’s work environment.

HR background check: a guide for job seekers and recruitment teams

Reference Check: Digging The Truth of Candidate’s Past Performance

Human and AI collaboration

 AI can process data rapidly, but human judgment remains essential for evaluating context and accuracy behind the data. At the same time, humans also have limitations. Therefore, collaboration between machine intelligence and human discernment is key to achieving accurate and objective results.

In practice, human involvement remains critical in:

  • Context analysis. Understanding the reasons behind findings that appear as red flags.
  • Data source validation. Ensuring that collected or used information comes from legal and reliable sources.
  • Legal and ethical compliance. Ensuring the screening process adheres to data protection laws, anti-discrimination policies, and other ethical standards.
  • Final review. Making recommendations based on contextual understanding, not merely on data or risk labels.

The future of employment background screening

While AI can efficiently handle repetitive and administrative tasks, humans are still required to interpret results, provide context, and make strategic decisions. This coexistence between AI and human intelligence offers the most effective and efficient solution for the future of the background screening industry.

The collaboration between humans and AI delivers distinct advantages such as:

  • Higher accuracy. Every AI-generated result is verified by human reviewers.
  • Enhanced legal compliance. Human oversight ensures full adherence to local and international regulations.
  • Fairer and wiser decisions for both candidates and employers.

Interestingly, the same study shows that several global companies including Siemens, Kaiser Permanente, Unilever, and Hilton have improved their hiring quality and efficiency through AI-human collaboration. AI handles the initial screening, while humans retain control over final decision-making. This collaborative approach not only speeds up recruitment but also ensures fairness, transparency, and alignment with organizational context.

Ultimately, both machine intelligence and human wisdom are indispensable in building a modern, accurate, and integrity-driven employment background screening process.

Title: A whistleblowing platform that people can actually trust
Author: Putri Pertiwi
Content:
Imagine you’re an employee who uncovers fraud, corruption, or abuse of power inside your organization. On paper, the company promises legal protection. Policies say “we support whistleblowers.” Posters talk about integrity. In reality, many people who speak up end up paying the price; losing their jobs, getting sidelined, being criminalized, or even receiving threats.

This isn’t speculation.

A recent case of a whistleblower in Indonesia who exposed corruption of public funds at the National Zakat Agency (BAZNAS) in West Java highlights a harsh truth that blowing the whistle often comes with retaliation. In addition, EY’s Global Integrity Report 2024 shows that more than half of respondents (51%) said they had faced or witnessed some form of retaliation or adverse consequences against someone who reported misconduct through their organization’s whistleblowing mechanism. 

As a result, employees hesitate. They weigh the risk. They ask themselves a difficult question: Do I want to do the right thing, or do I want to stay safe?

That hesitation is what kills early detection. And that’s why organizations cannot simply promise protection. They have to prove it with systems that are not symbolic, not easily compromised, and not built merely to meet compliance checklists.

They need a whistleblowing platform that people actually trust.

Why “checking a box” isn’t enough

Most companies treat whistleblowing like a legal chore. But if you’re just doing the bare minimum to stay compliant, you’re missing the point. Investors, regulators, and your own team are tired of “values” posters. They want to see what happens when things go wrong.

When you move past the corporate jargon and actually secure your reporting lines, you get three things:

  1. Truth, Not Gossip. If people actually believe they won’t be hunted down for speaking the truth, they’ll stop looking the other way when they see someone dipping into the till.

  2. A Head Start on Disasters. The ACFE estimates companies lose 5% of their revenue to fraud every year. It’s much cheaper to fix a problem when a whistleblower tips you off early than to wait for a federal investigation.

  3. Real Credibility. A reporting portal doesn’t prove you’re an ethical company, how you treat the person who uses it does.

‘Trust’ is the core currency of whistleblowing system

Whistleblowing is a high-stakes gamble. If an employee doesn’t trust the house, they won’t play. Studies show the number one reason people keep quiet is the fear of being identified and receiving retaliation. 

ACFE and The Institute of Internal Auditors (IAA) survey “Building a Best-in-Class Whistleblower Hotline 2023” highlights anonymity as top consideration for the success of a whistleblowing system within organizations. In addition, research by  the Ethics & Compliance Initiative shows that organizations with effective whistleblower programs reported up to 50% lower rates of fraud, demonstrating the trust factor’s impact on deterrence. 

These studies underline one point that is when employees trust that their identity will remain protected, they are far more likely to speak up, and that trust, in the end, translates into measurable reductions in misconduct.

However, most “secure” systems are still built on emails, hotlines, or portals that force you to create an account. To an employee, these aren’t reporting channels. They’re risk triggers. If the system itself feels unsafe, no amount of campaigns, posters, or slogans will convince employees otherwise.

An anonymous-enabled whistleblower platform

Canary Whistleblowing was designed with a clear purpose: to remove the psychological and operational barriers that stop employees from reporting wrongdoing.

Its key capability, Canary Mute, allows whistleblowers to remain completely anonymous while staying connected to the investigation process.

  • No personal details required. Whistleblowers do not need to share any personal contact information.
  • Secure access via unique credentials. Whistleblowers receive a combination of a report ID and a password, which they can use to re-enter the system.
  • Two-way communication enabled. Even while remaining anonymous, whistleblowers can receive updates on their case and respond to follow-up questions from investigators.

This system ensures confidentiality from start to finish. Whistleblowers can stay involved in the process, providing additional evidence, clarifications, or context, without ever exposing their identity.

Proof over promises

At the end of the day, a whistleblowing platform is not “just a reporting tool.” It is a real-world test of your organization’s integrity posture. Title: HR background check: a guide for job seekers and recruitment teams
Author: Putri Pertiwi
Content:
Background checks have become a crucial step in the recruitment process, especially to ensure that candidates truly possess the qualifications, track records, and integrity required by the company. Unfortunately, awareness of the importance of this process remains low, particularly among job seekers.

In a brief interview with visitors at our booth during France Alumni Day 2025, only 20% understood what a pre-employment background check is, and just 10% had heard about it from social media. This highlights an information gap on pre-employment background checks that needs to be addressed through broader education.

What is a background check?

A background check is the process of verifying the information listed in a candidate’s Curriculum Vitae (CV) and supporting documents submitted during the recruitment process. It is typically conducted by companies before making a final hiring decision. This process may include various aspects, such as:

  • Legitimacy of identity documents
  • Educational background
  • Employment history
  • Professional references
  • Criminal record
  • Digital footprint and social media activity
  • Credit history (for certain positions)

Through this thorough review, the HR team can assess whether the information provided by the candidate is accurate. This helps ensure that the candidate truly has the qualifications, integrity, and track record required for the role.

Why do companies conduct background checks?

Background checks are more than just a formality. They are a strategic measure to minimize risks that could negatively impact the company. Here are the main reasons HR teams conduct background checks:

  • Avoiding poor hiring decisions

 Hiring unqualified employees can lead to financial losses and reduced team productivity. It is essential to verify documents such as diplomas, certifications, and employment history. Direct confirmation with former supervisors also helps objectively assess the candidate’s performance and integrity.

  • Ensuring a safe and comfortable work environment

Checking criminal records, digital footprints, and social media activity helps ensure the candidate doesn’t have a history that could jeopardize safety or workplace ethics. This is especially critical for roles with access to sensitive or confidential information.

  • Ensuring regulatory compliance

In certain sectors—such as finance, healthcare, or education—background checks are mandatory to meet compliance and regulatory standards. Without this process, companies risk legal violations and potential penalties.

  • Protecting company reputation

Hiring employees with problematic backgrounds can damage the company’s reputation in the eyes of the public and business partners. Background checks help prevent such risks from the outset.

What should job seekers know?

For job seekers, understanding the background check process can be an advantage. Here are a few key points to keep in mind:

  • Integrity of your CV
    Avoid exaggerating your experience, job titles, or educational qualifications. Inaccurate information is easy to detect and may disqualify you.
  • Mind your digital footprint
    Many companies now also check social media profiles of potential employees. Make sure your accounts reflect thoughtful and well-curated content.
  • Prepare credible references
    HR will likely contact former supervisors or colleagues to gain insight into your performance.
  • Ensure your documents are complete and valid
    Your education certificates, employment letters, ID card, and other supporting documents will be verified for authenticity.

Tips for HR teams conducting background checks

For HR teams seeking to make background checks an integral part of recruitment, here are some steps to consider:

  1. Consent letter
    Before conducting a pre-employment background check, it is crucial to obtain the candidate’s written consent in the form of a consent letter. A consent letter grants formal permission for the company to verify personal details such as education, work history, and other records. It also ensures compliance with data protection regulations and builds transparency and trust between the company and the candidate.
  2. Use a professional background check service
    While background checks can be done in-house, the process can be time-consuming, require specific expertise, and carry the risk of bias if not conducted with the right methodology. That’s why many companies choose to use third-party services with experience and credibility in this field.

Why is this important?

    • Access to official and legal information sources
      Professional providers often have access to various verified local and international data sources, ensuring results are accurate, legal, and compliant with current regulations.
    • Expertise in cross-aspect verification
      Background checks go beyond simply verifying diplomas or employment history. Professional services can investigate other critical aspects, such as criminal records, digital footprints, and professional references.
    • Protecting compliance and data privacy
      Improper background checks can lead to legal risks, especially regarding privacy and personal data protection. Reliable providers are well-versed in these legal aspects, especially those accredited by the Professional Background Screening Association (PBSA).
    • Saving time and resources
      Outsourcing this process allows HR to focus on more strategic areas of recruitment and employee development.

One trusted provider of employment background checks in Indonesia is Integrity Indonesia. With over 20 years of experience in compliance, Integrity Indonesia has supported many national and multinational companies in verifying their candidates’ integrity.

Integrity Indonesia’s background screening services include:

The screening results are delivered in a comprehensive report structured to help HR teams make faster and more accurate decisions. The process prioritizes diligence, confidentiality, and compliance with data protection regulations. Contact us at info@integrity-asia.com or click here to learn more about our customized employment background check solutions.

    Not all background aspects are necessary for every position. Focus only on elements that directly affect the job. For example, for a finance staff position, relevant checks include educational and work history, criminal records, identity verification, and references from former supervisors to assess the candidate’s integrity and accuracy.

For job seekers, background checks are nothing to fear. In fact, they’re an opportunity to demonstrate professionalism and integrity. For HR teams, pre-employment screening is a strategic step in building a reliable, trustworthy, and capable workforce.

With mutual understanding from both sides, the recruitment process can become more transparent, fair, and efficient, paving the way for a healthier and more sustainable workplace.
